procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the management discharging R. K. Jain from service (order of discharge dated October 1, 1963)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madhya Pradesh High Court in Madhya Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Industrial Court, Madhya Pradesh held that after concluding that a domestic inquiry was improper, the Industrial Tribunal or Labour Court should give the employer an opportunity to produce evidence to justify their action. The Orissa High Court in Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. Their Workers through Rourkela Mazdoor Sabha and others, rejected the management's claim that the Labour Court should give notice about defects in the domestic inquiry and an opportunity to adduce independent evidence. A Single Judge of the Delhi High Court in Premnath Motors Workshop Private took a similar view to the Orissa High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (likely the bank) approached the Supreme Court contending that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the discharge order.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is mandatory for a Labour Tribunal to conduct a two-part inquiry, first determining the validity of the domestic inquiry as a preliminary issue, and only then proceeding to consider the merits of the charges by allowing parties to adduce fresh evidence.

law.fact: The inquiry conducted by a Labour Tribunal is a single, "composite inquiry" regarding the challenged order of termination or dismissal.
law.source: The inquiry that is conducted by the Tribunal is a composite inquiry, and there is no justification for the view that the inquiry before the Tribunal has to be conducted in two parts...

law.fact: The management has the right to defend its action in two ways: either by relying solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry, or by also adducing fresh evidence before the Tribunal to justify its action on the merits.
law.source: It is also open to the management to justify on facts that the order passed by it was proper... It is essentially a matter for the management to decide about the stand that it proposes to take before the Tribunal.

law.fact: If the management chooses to rely only on its domestic inquiry and the Tribunal finds it invalid, the management will lose the case.
law.source: If the management defends its action solely on the basis that the domestic inquiry held by it is proper and valid and if the Tribunal hokls against the management on that point, the management will fail.

law.fact: If the management adduces fresh evidence, the Tribunal can uphold the management's action based on that evidence, even if it finds the original domestic inquiry was invalid.
law.source: It is open to the Tribunal to accept the evidence adduced by the management to justify its action and hold in its favour even if its finding is against the management regarding the validity of the domestic inquiry.

law.fact: There is no mandatory rule that the validity of the domestic inquiry must be decided as a preliminary issue; this is a matter of discretion for the Tribunal.
law.source: In our opinion, no hard and fast rule can be laid down under what circumstance an issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue. That is a matter for the Tribunal or the Labour Court concerned to consider...

application.fact: The Court directly addressed a conflict of opinion between different High Courts on this procedural issue.
application.source: It is clear from the rthree decisions of the High Courts, referred to above, that there is a difference of view between the· Orissa High Court on the one hand and the Madhya Pradesh and Delhi High Courts on the other.

application.fact: The Court explicitly rejected the view of the Madhya Pradesh and Delhi High Courts, which held that the inquiry must be conducted in two parts.
application.source: The Madhya Pradesh and Delhi High Courts appear to proceed on rthe basis that the inquiry before 1he Tribunal has to be conducted in two parts... As already mentioned by us earlier, :there is no justification for such a view being taken.

application.fact: The Court reasoned that the core issue referred to a Tribunal is the broader question of whether the termination was justified, not merely the procedural correctness of the domestic inquiry.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that a two-part inquiry is mandatory. It held that the inquiry before a Labour Tribunal is a single, composite process. The management has the right to decide its strategy: it can either rely solely on its domestic inquiry or choose to present fresh evidence to justify its action on the merits. The Tribunal can uphold the management's decision based on this fresh evidence, even if the domestic inquiry was flawed. The Court concluded there is "no justification" for a mandatory two-part procedure and that deciding the validity of the domestic inquiry as a preliminary issue is a matter of discretion for the Tribunal, not a hard and fast rule.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is mandatory for a Labour Tribunal to conduct a two-part inquiry, first determining the validity of the domestic inquiry as a preliminary issue, and only then proceeding to consider the merits of the charges by allowing parties to adduce fresh evidence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (management) contended that the Tribunal, after finding the domestic inquiry to be invalid, should have then held a second stage of the proceedings to allow the management to adduce independent evidence to justify its disciplinary action on the merits of the charges.
respondent_arguments: The inquiry before the Tribunal is a single, composite inquiry. It is the management's choice and right to defend its action by relying on the domestic inquiry, adducing fresh evidence on the merits, or both, during this single proceeding. If the management chooses to rely solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry and fails on that point, it is not entitled to a second opportunity to present evidence on the merits, as it failed to avail itself of that right during the composite inquiry.

cases.case_name: Workmen of Motipur Sugar Factory (Private) Ltd. v. Motipur Sugar Factory
cases.principle: Cited as a precedent establishing the circumstances under which a Tribunal is justified in interfering with an order of discharge.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a domestic inquiry is found to be improper, the management has the right to adduce independent evidence before the Tribunal to justify its action. The inquiry before the Tribunal is a composite one, and it can uphold the management's action based on this evidence, even if the domestic inquiry was invalid. However, if the management defends its action solely on the validity of its domestic inquiry and that inquiry is found to be defective, the management will fail.
obiter: No hard and fast rule can be laid down regarding when an issue is to be decided as a preliminary issue; that is a matter for the Tribunal or Labour Court to consider based on the pleadings and points that arise.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the present case, the management's stand was that it was prepared to justify the legality of the order of discharge solely on the basis of the domestic inquiry held by it as a result of which the order of discharge was passed. It never offered to produce any evidence before the Tribunal apart from the inquiry proce<o rings. No opportunity for justifying its action was asked for by the management nor availed of.
legal_tests_applied: The termination of an employee's service must be preceded by a proper domestic inquiry held in accordance with the rules of natural justice. Therefore, it is evident •that if the inquiry is vitiated by violation of the principles of natural justice or if no reasonable opportunity was provided to a delinquent to place his defence, it cannot be characterized as a proper domestic inquiry held in accordance with the rules of natural justice.
why_appellant_lost: The management chose to justify the legality of the discharge order 'solely on the basis of the domestic inquiry held by it'.
The management 'never offered to produce any evidence before the Tribunal apart from the inquiry proce<o rings.'
The management never asked for, nor availed itself of, an 'opportunity for justifying its action' with fresh evidence during the Tribunal proceedings.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the implicit argument that the proceeding before the Tribunal is a single opportunity for the management to present its case, whether by relying on the domestic inquiry, adducing fresh evidence, or both.

The management made a strategic choice to rely exclusively on its domestic inquiry and, having failed on that ground, was not entitled to a second opportunity to present evidence on the merits which it had failed to do during the main proceeding.
policy_considerations: The ruling implicitly discourages piecemeal litigation by requiring a party to present its entire case, including alternative positions (like adducing fresh evidence on the merits), during the single composite inquiry before the Tribunal, rather than allowing a party to seek a second chance after its primary legal strategy has failed.
